Learning Objectives
Understand the pathophysiology of diabetic foot ulceration and infection.
Understand how to evaluate and diagnose a patient with a diabetic foot ulceration and
infection and how to differentiate infection from arthropathy.
Apply major methods of nonsurgical management for diabetic foot ulceration and infection.
Understand surgical indications and treatment options for the management of diabetic foot
ulceration and infection and the surgical outcomes and potential complications.

The pathologic process that leads to and maintains diabetic foot ulceration is complex and
multifactorial, with contributions from diabetic peripheral neuropathy, diabetic vascular
disease, Charcot arthropathic deformity, and immune suppression.
The loss of protective sensation in combination with peripheral vascular disease likely are the
most important factors.
Bacteria spread through superficial cracks in the skin or into deep ulcerations may result in
soft-tissue abscess or bony infection.

Overview
The pathologic process that initiates and maintains diabetic foot disease is complex and
multifactorial.1-4 Elevated blood glucose levels result in microvascular disease leading to
diabetic peripheral neuropathy. This impaired sensation inhibits the withdrawal reflex
and leaves the foot vulnerable to pressure and shear forces of a greater magnitude than
those normally experienced.5 Diabetic neuropathy also preferentially inhibits stimuli to
the smaller muscles of the lower extremity, most notably the dorsiflexors of the foot and
ankle, leading to dynamic motor imbalance (Figure 1). This results in equinus during
terminal stance, which places increased pressure on the plantar aspects of the
metatarsal heads, stressing the soft tissue in that location. Diabetes mellitus also leads
to vasomotor neuropathy, which involves swelling of the soft tissues and diminished
tissue lubrication. These swollen and poorly lubricated tissues are less effective
absorbers of pressure and repetitive microtrauma and, therefore, are more likely to fail
via ulceration. Vasomotor neuropathy also diminishes the ability of sweat glands to
moisturize the skin, causing brittleness and cracks that serve as entry portals for
bacterial infections. In patients with Charcot arthropathy, diminished touch, pain, and
proprioceptive sensation with respect to the joints of the foot and ankle and increased
blood flow as a result of arteriovenous shunting lead to traumatic arthropathy,
osteopenia, and fracture. These result in deformity, which, particularly in patients with
midfoot Charcot arthropathy and the associated rocker-bottom foot, result in localized
plantar pressure increases, predisposing to ulceration (Figure 2).

Confluence of some or all of these factors allows for repetitive low-level loading or a
single moderately severe injury to break skin, with an impaired ability to generate an
effective healing response, resulting in ulceration (Figure 3). Footwear is a major factor,

shows the foot of a patient with a metatarsophalangeal ulceration under the hallux.
Plantar view (B) and medial view (C) clinical photographs of the foot of a patient show

In patients with severe peripheral vascular disease that is worse than the neuropathy,
gangrene of the toes or ischemic ulceration of the plantar forefoot or the toe tips may be
the predominant inciting factors for a foot ulcer (rather than increased pressure and
shear forces). In these patients, vascular consultation and potential restoration of
vascularity may be the priority.

Epidemiology and Microbiology
Affects approximately 12% of patients with diabetes mellitus
Responsible for approximately 85% of lower-extremity amputations in patients with diabetes
mellitus; most common medical complication for which patients with diabetes mellitus seek
treatment
Diabetic infections usually are polymicrobial.
The most common pathogens are aerobic gram-positive cocci (especially Staphylococcus
aureus); gram-negative rods may be present in patients with chronic wounds or those recently
managed via antibiotic agents.
Obligate anaerobic pathogens may cause infection in patients with foot ischemia or gangrene.
Deep cultures and tissue biopsy may be necessary for diagnosis.

Epidemiology and Microbiology
Diabetic foot ulceration, foot infection, and Charcot neuropathy are major sources of
morbidity and mortality for patients with diabetes mellitus.1 Approximately 4% of the
population with diabetes mellitus has a foot ulceration or infection at any given time,
and the lifetime prevalence of diabetic foot infections is 15%. Diabetic foot ulcerations
precede almost all diabetic lower-extremity amputations, with more than 70,000 diabetic
lower-extremity amputations performed per year. More than one-third of patients
undergoing a lower-extremity amputation because of complications of diabetes mellitus
will not survive the subsequent 2 years.7
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
A comprehensive patient history should focus on the foot and ankle, paying special attention
to tobacco use, prior treatment, diabetic management, and medical comorbidities.
Pain may or may not be a presenting complaint.


Patient History
By the time patients progress to the point of a foot ulceration, infection, or neuropathic
joints, they generally have involvement of multiple organ systems and global
immunodeficiency.1,4 Patients may or may not report pain associated with the diabetic
foot disease because of a loss in peripheral sensation. Consultation and collaboration
with medical colleagues are critical. Foot ulcers may have been present for variable
durations, with progression or regression. Infections commonly present more acutely,
with a warm swollen foot with or without a draining wound. Differentiation of infection
from acute Charcot neuropathy may be difficult based on patient history alone. Patient
history must be supplemented by a physical examination and common laboratory and
imaging studies.
Physical Examination and Classification
Ulceration examination
Ulcers can be described according to the Meggitt-Wagner classification.
Grade 0: no open lesion
Grade 1: superficial lesion
Grade 2: deep ulcer (through dermis)
Grade 3: abscess/osteomyelitis
Grade 4: partial foot gangrene
Grade 5: whole foot gangrene
Ulcers also can be described according to Brodsky’s depth-ischemia classification, which
allows for independent characterization of ulcer depth and vascular status.
Depth
Grade 0: no break in skin
Grade 1: superficial ulcer
Grade 2: exposed tendons, joints
Grade 3: exposed bone and/or abscess/osteomyelitis
Ischemia
Grade A: no ischemia
Grade B: ischemia not gangrenous

Grade C: partial foot gangrene
Grade D: complete gangrene
A cotton-tipped applicator is used to test for the ability to probe to bone, which represents a
deep ulcer.
Vascular evaluation
More than 60% of diabetic ulcers have diminished blood flow secondary to peripheral
vascular disease; therefore, a vascular examination is critical.
Vascular examination includes:
Assessment of the dorsalis pedis and tibialis pulses
Examination of the condition of the skin, noting the absence of hair on the feet and toes
If the physical examination indicates additional evaluation, the ankle-brachial index, Doppler
ultrasonography with digital arterial pressures, transcutaneous toe oxygen measurement,
and arteriography can be performed.
An ankle-brachial index of at least 0.45 and toe pressures greater than 40 mm Hg are
necessary to heal an ulcer in a diabetic foot.
Transcutaneous oxygen measurements greater than 30 mm Hg indicate that blood flow is
adequate for healing.

Physical Examination and Classification
The overall severity of illness dictates the urgency of treatment in patients with a diabetic
foot ulceration or infection.1,4,8 In patients with a fever, an increased circulating glucose
level, or an elevated insulin requirement, infection is likely, and treatment prudent to
avoid escalation; sepsis; and, potentially, circulatory collapse. If a foot lacks a break in
the soft tissue but is warm and erythematous without clinical signs of sepsis, then
Charcot arthropathy is more likely than deep infection. Another key physical
examination finding that helps differentiate Charcot arthropathy from infection is the
dependent nature of edema and erythema associated with Charcot arthropathy, such
that elevation will improve edema and erythema but not osteomyelitis or abscess in a
patient with Charcot arthropathy.4 Patients with diabetes mellitus are
immunocompromised and, therefore, may not have a fever or other systemic signs of
sepsis, even in the setting of virulent infection. Therefore, systemic and circulatory
decompensation may be rapid and occur with little warning.

In most patients, signs of sepsis will be absent, and patients simply will present for
management of a chronic foot ulceration.1 Dorsal wounds often are the result of direct
trauma or poorly fitting shoes. Plantar ulcerations tend to occur beneath the metatarsal
heads, the base of the fifth metatarsal, the heel, or under a plantar exostosis.
The Meggitt-Wagner (Table 1)8-10 and Brodsky (Figure 4)4 classifications can be used to
describe the nature and severity of the diabetic foot, with the Brodsky classification
allowing for independent characterization of the vascular and ulcer depth status of the
disease.4,8 These grading systems also can be used to guide management. Wounds with
purulent drainage or necrotic tissue mandate thorough débridement at a minimum. If
erythema surrounds the wound, then osteomyelitis, abscess, or cellulitis is likely (Figure
5; Resource 1).

No role exists for superficial swab culture or material in patients with a Wagner grade 1
or grade 2 ulceration because they will be contaminated by irrelevant microbes from the
outside environment.1,4 Grade 3 wounds are, by definition, abscesses that should be
managed surgically; deep-tissue cultures are more relevant for such ulcerations;
therefore, they can and should be obtained.
A Semmes-Weinstein 5.07 monofilament can be used to confirm the presence of diabetic
peripheral neuropathy; however, this usually is implicit in patients with a nonhealing
ulceration.
Imaging and Laboratory Studies
Laboratory Studies for Wound-Healing Ability
Patients with nonhealing wounds often are malnourished.
Examine for evidence of osteomyelitis or soft-tissue infection
The accepted wound-healing levels are a serum albumin level of 3.0 g/dL and a total
lymphocyte count higher than 1,500/mm3.
Laboratory Studies for Acute or Chronic Infection
White blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level may be
useful in ruling out/in infection but are nonspecific.
Patients with severe diabetes mellitus often are immunocompromised and may fail to mount
an inflammatory response, rendering these laboratory values less useful.
Radiography
Weight-bearing AP, lateral, and oblique radiographs of the foot and ankle
Examine for evidence of osteomyelitis or soft-tissue infection

Radiography

Plain weight-bearing radiographs, including three views of the foot and three views of
the ankle, should be examined for evidence of osteomyelitis or soft-tissue infection.1,4,11
Osteomyelitis is suggested by loss of the normal trabecular cancellous bone pattern,
bone destruction, or periosteal reaction.11 Soft-tissue infection is suggested by soft-
tissue swelling observed on radiographs; however, this finding is nonspecific.
Advanced Imaging Studies
The main advantage of advanced imaging is to identify evidence of deep-tissue infection (bony
or soft tissue).
MRI may aid in the diagnosis of osteomyelitis and/or an abscess but may not distinguish
between Charcot arthropathy and infection with a high specificity.
Nuclear studies using technetium Tc-99m, gallium Ga-67, or indium In-111 may help
differentiate between soft-tissue infection and osteomyelitis, Charcot arthropathy, or a
combination of infection and Charcot arthropathy.

Advanced Imaging Studies
Clinical examination and plain radiography are the mainstay of treatment for most
patients with diabetic foot disease. Advanced imaging studies are necessary to rule out
osteomyelitis and abscesses in select patients.12
MRI and bone scintigraphy are imaging options to help differentiate Charcot arthropathy
from diabetic foot infection.1,11-14 Three-phase Tc-99m scintigraphy in combination with
In-111–labeled leukocyte scanning are associated with a sensitivity near 100% and a
specificity of approximately 80% with regard to differentiating osteomyelitis from
Charcot arthropathy. Studies suggest that MRI is less specific than three-phase Tc-99m
scintigraphy in combination with In-111-labeled leukocyte scanning with regard to the
detection of osteomyelitis. However, MRI, which is associated with excellent soft-tissue
resolution, is superior to bone scanning in identifying associated soft-tissue abscess. MRI
also is easier to perform and is not associated with radiation exposure. MRI has emerged
as the best advanced imaging modality for the detection of bone involvement and soft-

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Wagner grade 1 or grade 2 ulceration
Braceable or stage 0, stage 1, or stage 2 Charcot arthropathy
Superficial infection
Contraindications
Deep infection
Systemic sepsis
Late-stage Charcot deformity not amenable to bracing
Techniques/Procedures
In-office débridement—Sharp débridement of necrotic tissue down to a clean tissue base
often results in healing
Local wound care—The dressing should accomplish the following goals:
Provide a moist environment
Absorb exudates
Act as a barrier
Offload pressure
Provide antibiosis (occasionally required)
Offloading
Total contact casting—the preferred method of offloading
Pneumatic walking brace—A prefabricated brace can be used to decrease forefoot and
midfoot plantar pressure.
Advantages—Allows for more frequent wound surveillance, allows for several types of
dressings, easy to apply

Disadvantages—Severe foot deformity makes the use of a pneumatic walking brace
difficult, and patient compliance may be suboptimal.
Shoes—Off-the-shelf shoes with or without modifications; should have rocker sole, extra
depth, high and wide toe box, and accommodative insole
Custom shoes
Therapeutic shoes
In 1998, Congress signed the Therapeutic Shoe Bill into law after studies showed potential
net Medicare savings by preventing diabetic foot complications.
Qualified patients include those being medically treated for diabetes mellitus with a history
of neuropathy with callus, past ulcerations, foot deformity, past amputation, or poor
circulation.
The Therapeutic Shoe Bill covers one pair of custom-molded shoes per year, with a total of
three inserts or one pair of qualifying depth shoes with three inserts.

Nonsurgical Management
Most patients present to an orthopaedic surgeon for treatment without systemic signs of
infection or deeply infected wounds. The common reason patients seeking care in this
setting is a chronic or newly discovered nonhealing wound with or without previous
management. The probe-to-bone test is used in these patients to determine ulcer depth
(Wagner grade 1 versus grade 2). Thick callus and necrotic tissue can be removed in the
clinic with the use of a scalpel without inciting pain. Grade 1 and grade 2 wounds with
cellulitis can be empirically managed via a first-generation cephalosporin or other
antibiotic agent to augment this office-based treatment (Table 2).

The key to the nonsurgical management of diabetic foot ulcerations is offloading.1,4,15-17
Offloading refers to the distribution of local pressure across an increased surface area.16
This can be achieved with the use of a total contact cast (Video 1), pneumatic walking
brace (Charcot restraint orthosis walker; Figure 6), or therapeutic shoe (Figure 7),
depending on severity of the ulcer, stage of healing, and tolerance of the patient. Total
contact casting is the preferred method for offloading diabetic foot ulcers and also
afford soft-tissue protection and bony stabilization of Charcot arthropathy. Patients with
grade 3 or higher ulcers should undergo incision, drainage, and antibiotic therapy, with
wound improvement before cast application. Casts should be changed every 2 to 4
weeks until erythema and edema have resolved and the temperature of the affected
limb has decreased and becomes similar to that of the contralateral limb. Ulcers should
be evaluated, and débridement should be performed at the time of cast changes.
Pneumatic walking braces offer an alternative for neuropathic ulceration or Charcot
arthropathy. Pneumatic walking braces allow for more frequent wound surveillance and
dressing changes; however, severe foot deformity makes ambulation in these braces
difficult, and patient compliance is low. For patients with ulcers that have healed,
increased-depth, custom-molded shoes with custom inserts typically are the long-term
strategy for decreasing the risk of recurrence. Typically, they can be funded through the
Therapeutic Shoe Bill.6

Surgical Management
Indications
Deep infection
Systemic sepsis
Late-stage Charcot deformity not amenable to bracing
Wagner grade 3 ulceration
Deep abscess
Exposed tendon and/or bone
Positive probe-to-bone test
Nonhealing superficial ulceration despite nonsurgical management
Techniques/Procedures
Achilles tendon lengthening
For patients with forefoot overload, Achilles tendon lengthening or gastrocnemius recession
may relieve forefoot pressures during the latter portion of the stance phase of gait.
Formal Achilles tendon lengthening (triple-cut hemi-section or open) or gastrocnemius
recession is preferred to Achilles tendon transection because Achilles tendon transection
may result in a calcaneal gait and heel ulceration (Figure 8).

hallux ulceration. The patient was treated via amputation and Achilles tendon transection,
which resulted in a calcaneal gait and heel ulceration. (Images courtesy of Lew Schon, MD,
Baltimore, MD.)
Débridement
Drainage of deep infections often is necessary to prevent tissue necrosis, free the area of
infection, and achieve wound-healing without tension.
Before antibiotic treatment is initiated, specimens for culture should be obtained via biopsy,
ulcer curettage, or aspiration rather than via wound swab.
Osteomyelitis is present in 67% of patients with an ulcer that can be probed to bone.
Antibiotic beads can be used to help eradicate infection after débridement of osteomyelitis.
Negative pressure wound therapy can be used to facilitate healing after débridement.
Exostectomy or realignment arthrodesis

Exostectomy or realignment arthrodesis may be necessary to remove the internal pressure
caused by bony prominences.
This is particularly common in Charcot arthropathy.
Achilles tendon lengthening may help reduce plantar forefoot pressure.
Arthrodesis fixation can be achieved via internal or external fixation.
Amputation
To achieve a clean wound bed in patients with a massive ulceration, deep abscess, or bony
infection, partial or total foot amputation may be required.
Amputation level is dictated by the ability to completely eradicate infected tissue (bony and
soft tissue) and the ability to achieve soft-tissue coverage via primary closure.
Specific amputations and increases in energy expenditures:
Toe amputation
Ray resection
Transmetatarsal
Lisfranc
Chopart
Syme
Transtibial

Surgical Management
Wagner grade 3 wounds are those with deep abscess or osteomyelitis (ie, any wound
with exposed tendon or bone or a positive probe-to-bone test qualifies).1,4 This is the
most common indication for surgical management of a diabetic foot ulceration. At a
minimum, débridement, intraoperative culture, and culture-directed antibiotic therapy
are required. The goal is conversion to a clean wound bed and healing via primary
closure or secondary intention. To achieve a clean wound bed, partial or total foot
amputation may be required. In patients who undergo osseous débridement, antibiotic
agents can be delivered directly to the surgical site with the use of antibiotic-
impregnated cement beads or spacers.18 Negative pressure wound therapy can be used
to facilitate healing after débridement.19 For wounds that are closed primarily, the
closed incision or incisional vacuum-assisted closure technique can be used. For wounds
that cannot be closed primarily, the open incision or traditional wound vacuum-assisted

a suitable wound bed for healing via secondary intention; additional osseus resection is
recommended in such patients.
In addition to débridement and amputation, Achilles tendon lengthening/gastrocnemius
recession, exostectomy, and realignment arthrodesis are the other three major
procedures for management of the diabetic foot. Exostectomy is commonly indicated in
patients with midfoot arch collapse from Charcot arthropathy that results in a plantar
bony midfoot prominence preventing healing of a plantar ulcer.20 In these patients, a
plantarmedial, plantarlateral, or direct plantar approach via the ulcer or via a separate
incision is used to resect the offending bony prominence. However, simple exostectomy
is insufficient for many patients with greater deformity. In these patients, realignment
arthrodesis is required. The specific arthrodesis will vary based on the location of the
deformity; however, it may involve the midfoot, Chopart joint, hindfoot, and/or tibiotalar
joint. Fixation can be achieved via internal fixation, external fixation, or both. Advantages
of external fixation include single-stage procedure, even in the presence of infection or
ulceration; access for soft-tissue monitoring; and no or limited internal hardware. Early–
weight bearing, although it occurs inadvertently, is not advised in patients with
neuropathy because the pins may break or become infected as a result of excessive
motion and microtrauma.
Débridement, amputation, exostectomy, and realignment arthrodesis can be performed
in combination with Achilles tendon lengthening or gastrocnemius recession to further
offload the plantar forefoot during toe-off.15,21,22 Achilles tendon (triple-cut hemi-
section or open) or gastrocnemius recession also can be performed in isolation or in
combination with total contact casting or other forms of offloading. In general,
transection of the Achilles tendon should be avoided because weakened or no plantar
flexion power may result in a calcaneus gait and a heel ulcer (Figure 8).
Every effort is made to achieve limb salvage via nonsurgical management, wound
débridement, exostectomy, vascular intervention, and deformity correction; however,
occasionally this is not possible.23,24 The goal then shifts to providing the patient with an
extremity that is maximally functional with the use of a prosthesis. Amputation level is

dictated by the ability to completely eradicate necrotic and infected tissue (bone and soft

In general, more proximal amputations require a greater increase in energy expenditure
with ambulation. A notable exception to this is that Lisfranc and Chopart amputations
paradoxically require more energy expenditure than Syme amputations. Mechanical
consequences to amputation include stress transfers to other sites and loss of tendon
function, which may play a role in future breakdowns. A first ray amputation may resect
the tibialis anterior tendon and result in a footdrop. Lisfranc amputation removes the
insertion of the peroneus brevis, which should be transferred, if infection permits, to the
lateral midfoot to achieve inversion/eversion (or coronal) balance. Similarly, Chopart
amputation removes the insertion of the tibialis anterior, which should be transferred, if
infection permits, to the dorsal talar neck to achieve sagittal balance.
